meta.title: Who really said "Be nice to nerds. Chances are you'll end up working for one"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The punchline of a list of rules forwarded for years as a Bill Gates speech. Wikiquote credits the list to the writer Charles J. Sykes.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be nice to nerds. Chances are you'll end up working for one'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Bill Gates. Wikiquote says the list of blunt school rules is based on one from the American author Charles J. Sykes.

answer.label: Not Bill Gates — actually Charles J. Sykes
answer.authorDates: Born 1954 · American author and political commentator
answer.sourceLine: The joke is the reason the whole list stuck to Bill Gates’s name — a software billionaire telling teenagers to be kind to nerds is almost too neat. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗ and credits the list to Charles J. Sykes; we could not establish which of his works first carried it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Bill Gates, in a high-school speech

source.excerpt: Life is not fair. Get used to it... Be nice to nerds. Chances are you'll end up working for one.
trail: Wikiquote’s Bill Gates page ↗ lists this line under Misattributed, and says that although the list is widely attributed to Gates on the internet, it “is actually based on one from Charles J. Sykes”.
Wikiquote’s note points to a Snopes fact-check for the fuller story. That page is unreachable from our network, so we have not read it and do not repeat its findings here.

Sykes is a real and identifiable writer — his bibliography ↗ includes Dumbing Down Our Kids (1995) and 50 Rules Kids Won’t Learn in School (2007) — but we could not confirm which work first published this list, so no specific work is claimed here.
source.excerptNote: The wording above is the entry exactly as it stands in Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗, which quotes this line together with the opening rule of the same list.
source.rightsNote: No copyright status is asserted, because we could not tie this wording to a specific publication. If the list is Charles J. Sykes’s, as Wikiquote says, it would be modern and in copyright; the version that circulates under Gates’s name has no identified publisher at all.

author.name: Charles J. Sykes
author.heading: About Charles J. Sykes
author.metaLine: Born 1954 · American author, radio host and political commentator
author.bio: Charles Jay Sykes (born 11 November 1954 in Seattle) is an American author and political commentator. He hosted a conservative talk show on Milwaukee’s WTMJ from 1993 to 2016 and later served as editor-in-chief of The Bulwark. His books on American schooling include Dumbing Down Our Kids (1995) and 50 Rules Kids Won’t Learn in School (2007).

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is the line that sold the hoax. Attach it to the founder of Microsoft and the whole list acquires a punchline and an author at the same time.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the line under Misattributed ↗, noting that although it is widely attributed to Gates on the internet, the list is not his.

misattribution.truthLine: Wikiquote credits the list to the writer Charles J. Sykes, not to Bill Gates — see the entry ↗. No specific Sykes work is claimed here, because we could not confirm one.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Of all the rules on the list, this is the one that made the attribution feel self-evidently right. The nerd who became the richest man alive, telling schoolchildren who their future boss would be — the line and the name explain each other.
That mutual fit is exactly why the misattribution was so hard to shake. A quote that sounds like its supposed author is one nobody thinks to check.
detailsBody: Wikiquote quotes this line and “Life is not fair. Get used to it…” together in a single entry, treating them as two rules from one circulating list rather than as separate sayings — which is how they travel.
context.pull: A quote that sounds like its author is one nobody thinks to check.
